abstract: Mercer's Global Talent Trends 2026 report, published February 25, 2026, surveys ~12,000 C-suite executives, HR leaders, investors, and employees across markets. The report finds AI is reshaping the wage-and-skills landscape: 65% of employers expect 11-30% of their workforce to be redeployed or reskilled due to AI within two years, 63% of employees would trade a 10% pay increase for AI/digital upskilling opportunities, and 72% of investors believe companies integrating human+AI capabilities gain competitive advantage. The report signals sharp compensation divergence: skilled-trades and frontline roles command premium wage growth while tech/professional-services compensation cools.
keyFindings: 12,000 respondents (C-suite, HR leaders, investors, employees) surveyed Sep-Oct 2025
65% of employers expect 11-30% of workforce redeployed or reskilled due to AI within 2 years
63% of employees would trade a 10% pay increase for opportunities to upskill in AI and digital skills
72% of investors believe companies combining human+AI capabilities gain competitive advantage
40% of employees worried about job loss from AI, up from 28% in 2024
59% of HR leaders cite difficulty attracting digital-skills talent as top challenge
77% of investors more likely to support companies committed to AI education
44% of employees report thriving at work (down from 66% in 2024)
Average 2026 merit budget projected at 3.2%; total salary budget 3.5%
Compensation growth in technology and professional services cooling as hiring normalizes
methodology: Global cross-sectional survey conducted by Mercer (part of Marsh McLennan) between September-October 2025, sample ~12,000 respondents across 4 stakeholder groups (C-suite, HR leaders, investors, employees). 11th annual edition; results weighted across 16 industries and 25+ countries.
qualifiers: Mercer is a Tier 2 institutional/consulting analyst — perspective is employer- and investor-facing. Numbers reflect self-reported attitudes and plans (not observed wage outcomes). Wage-premium implications are indirect: the report signals employers' willingness-to-pay for AI skills through the tech/professional-services compensation cooling and the skills-tradeoff data, rather than measuring realized AI wage premiums.
